subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire?

options.label: A
options.text: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.

options.label: B
options.text: The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.

options.label: C
options.text: The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.

options.label: D
options.text: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.

solution:
The magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are **concentric circles centred on the wire**, lying in planes perpendicular to it. Their direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule, and the circles grow larger and the field weaker as the distance from the wire increases.

The iron-filings pattern of the book's own activity shows exactly these circles. The other three options describe field shapes that belong to other situations — radial lines, for instance, describe an electric field around a point charge, not this magnetic field.
groundedIn: §12.2.1 Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor, and the right-hand thumb rule of §12.2.2.

stem: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
solution:
A short circuit happens when the **live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact** — usually because the insulation is damaged or an appliance is faulty.

The current then bypasses the appliance and flows through a path of almost **zero resistance**. By Ohm's law \(I = V/R\), a very small resistance across the same 220 V gives a very large current, so the current **increases heavily**. That surge is what melts the fuse and breaks the circuit.
groundedIn: §12.4 — 'Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact... the current in the circuit abruptly increases. This is called short-circuiting.'

subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
context: State whether the following statements are true or false.
stem: The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
solution:
**True.**

A long circular coil of many turns is a **solenoid**. The field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid are parallel straight lines, which is the sign that the field there is **uniform** — the same in magnitude and direction at every point inside.

It is also why a solenoid can be used to magnetise a piece of soft iron placed inside it, producing an electromagnet.
groundedIn: §12.2.4 — 'The field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines... the field is uniform inside the solenoid.'

context: State whether the following statements are true or false.
stem: A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
groundedIn: §12.4 Domestic Electric Circuits — the red, black and green colour code of the live, neutral and earth wires.

stem: List two methods of producing magnetic fields.
solution:
- **Using a permanent magnet.** A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding any magnet — a bar magnet or a horse-shoe magnet — and can be detected by the force it exerts on a compass needle.
- **Passing an electric current through a conductor.** Any current-carrying wire has a magnetic field associated with it. Winding the wire into a solenoid and placing a soft-iron core inside gives a strong field — an **electromagnet**.
groundedIn: §12.1 for the field of a magnet, and §12.2 and §12.2.4 for the field produced by an electric current and by a solenoid.

stem: When is the force experienced by a current–carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
solution:
The force is largest when the **direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field**.

The book's own experiment shows this: the displacement of the rod is greatest — that is, the magnitude of the force is highest — when current and field are mutually perpendicular. In that condition the direction of the force is perpendicular to both, and is given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

(When the current is parallel to the field, the force is zero.)
groundedIn: §12.3 — 'the displacement of the rod is largest (or the magnitude of the force is the highest) when the direction of current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.'

stem: Imagine that you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of magnetic field?
solution:
The magnetic field is directed **vertically downwards**.

Apply **Fleming's left-hand rule**, and be careful with one step that decides the whole answer: the beam is made of **electrons**, which are negatively charged, so the direction of **conventional current is opposite to the direction of motion**.

- The electrons travel from the back wall towards the front wall, so the **current** is directed from the front wall towards the back wall — that is, towards you.
- The **force** on the beam is towards your **right**.
- Setting the second finger along the current and the thumb along the force, the first finger — the field — points **downwards**.

So the magnetic field acts vertically downwards. Forgetting to reverse the current for a negative charge gives exactly the opposite answer, which is the trap in this question.
groundedIn: §12.3 — Fleming's left-hand rule, and the note in Example 12.2 that 'the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons'.

stem: State the rule to determine the direction of a (i) magnetic field produced around a straight conductor-carrying current, (ii) force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field which is perpendicular to it, and (iii) current induced in a coil due to its rotation in a magnetic field.
solution:
**(i) Right-hand thumb rule.** Hold the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the direction of the current; your fingers then wrap around the conductor in the direction of the magnetic field lines. (It is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule.)

**(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule.** Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of the force, or motion, of the conductor.

**(iii) Fleming's right-hand rule.** Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the thumb along the direction of motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current.

Note that part (iii) concerns electromagnetic induction, which this rationalised edition of the chapter no longer covers — which is also why the book's own answers list gives only (i) and (ii).
groundedIn: §12.2.2 for the right-hand thumb rule and §12.3 for Fleming's left-hand rule.

stem: When does an electric short circuit occur?
solution:
A short circuit occurs when the **live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact**.

This happens when the **insulation of the wires is damaged**, or when there is a **fault in an appliance**. The current then finds a path of almost zero resistance and bypasses the appliance, so the current in the circuit **increases abruptly**.

That sudden surge is dangerous — it can start a fire — which is why a fuse is placed in series with the circuit to melt and break it first.
groundedIn: §12.4 — 'Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. (This occurs when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance.)'

stem: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
solution:
**Function of the earth wire.** The earth wire has green insulation and is connected to a metal plate buried deep in the earth near the house. It provides a **low-resistance conducting path** from the appliance to the earth.

**Why metallic appliances must be earthed.** Appliances with a metallic body — an electric press, a toaster, a table fan, a refrigerator — can develop a fault in which the live wire touches the metal casing. Without earthing, that casing would be at a high potential, and anyone touching it would receive a **severe electric shock**.

With the casing connected to the earth wire, any leakage of current flows straight to the earth along the low-resistance path. The potential of the metallic body is kept at that of the earth, so the user is not shocked. The large leakage current also blows the fuse, cutting off the supply.
groundedIn: §12.4 — the earth wire 'provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current... ensures that any leakage of current to the metallic body of the appliance keeps its potential to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.'
